<reason>Side A won a competitive debate by making the proposition’s “even if” the actual decision rule. A uncoupled 2015 haze and peat crime from legal mineral-soil planting, offered enforcement tools that do not rewrite lawful expansion, and forced B to name frontier losers while admitting the rule still stands if compensation never arrives. That concession broke B’s debts-versus-deletions frame. B’s irreversibility argument stayed live and rhetorically strong, but the early rebrand of existing bans as the motion and the leftover tension between “targeted screening” and uncompensated income cuts left A with the cleaner reason to reject the motion as written.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A’s pressure on lawful losers and unpaid grants, then B’s admission that some frontier planting still stops even if the check never comes, which A converted into the closing comparison: this is not fire enforcement, it is taking a lawful hectare and keeping the rule when compensation fails.</best_rebuttal>
